title: Projective and global dimension are well defined
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-module and $m\ge n\ge0$ integers. (1) If $0\to P_n\to\dots\to P_0\to M\to0$ is an exact sequence of $R$-modules with every $P_i$ projective (a projective resolution of $M$ of length $\le n$), then putting $P_i=0$ for $n<i\le m$ gives an exact sequence $0\to P_m\to\dots\to P_0\to M\to0$ with all $P_i$ projective, i.e. a projective resolution of length $\le m$. (2) If $M$ has a projective resolution of length $\le n$ for some $n\ge0$, then there is a least integer $d\ge0$ such that $M$ has a projective resolution of length $\le d$, and for every $k\ge0$: $M$ has a projective resolution of length $\le k$ if and only if $d\le k$. (3) If there is an $n\ge0$ such that every $R$-module has a projective resolution of length $\le n$, then there is a least such integer $g\ge0$, and for every $k\ge0$: every $R$-module has a projective resolution of length $\le k$ if and only if $g\le k$.

proof.text: (1) Padding by zeros. Let $0\to P_n\xrightarrow{d_n}P_{n-1}\to\dots\to P_0\xrightarrow{d_0}M\to0$ be exact with every $P_i$ projective, and $m\ge n$; if $m=n$ there is nothing to do. Otherwise put $P_i=0$ for $n<i\le m$, with all maps out of and into these zero modules equal to $0$. The zero module is projective [def-weil-pbc-projective-module]: it is a direct summand of the free module $R^{\oplus\emptyset}=0$ (take $i=s=0$, then $s\circ i=0=\mathrm{id}_0$). The new sequence $0\to P_m\to\dots\to P_{n+1}\to P_n\to\dots\to P_0\to M\to0$ is a complex [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence]: every composite of two consecutive maps either is one of the original sequence, hence $0$, or passes through a zero module, hence is $0$. Exactness: at each new $P_i=0$ ($n<i\le m$) image and kernel are submodules of the zero module, hence both $0$ and equal. At $P_n$ the incoming map is now $P_{n+1}=0\to P_n$, with image $0$, exactly as the incoming map $0\to P_n$ of the original sequence; the outgoing map ($d_n$, or $d_0:P_0\to M$ when $n=0$) is unchanged; so exactness at $P_n$ is the original exactness there, i.e. $\operatorname{Ker}(d_n)=0$. At $P_i$ for $i<n$ and at $M$ both neighbouring maps are unchanged, so exactness there is the original one. Hence the padded sequence is a projective resolution of $M$ of length $\le m$.

proof.text: (2) Existence of the least length. Let $S_M=\{k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}: M\text{ has a projective resolution of length}\le k\}$. By hypothesis $n\in S_M$, so $S_M$ is a nonempty set of natural numbers and has a least element $d$ (least number principle for $\mathbb N$: if $S_M$ had no least element, induction on $j$ would show that no $k\le j$ lies in $S_M$ for every $j$, contradicting $n\in S_M$). By definition of $S_M$, $M$ has a projective resolution of length $\le d$, and $d\le k$ for every $k\in S_M$.

proof.text: (2) The equivalence. Let $k\ge0$. If $d\le k$, take a projective resolution of $M$ of length $\le d$ (Step 2) and pad it by zeros to length $\le k$ by Step 1; so $M$ has a projective resolution of length $\le k$. Conversely, if $M$ has a projective resolution of length $\le k$, then $k\in S_M$, so $d\le k$ by the minimality of $d$ (Step 2).

source.place: Algebra, Definition Tag 00O4 (definition-finite-proj-dim) and Definition Tag 00O6 (definition-finite-gl-dim); the minima are stated there without proof

proof.text: (3) Existence of the least global bound. Let $G=\{k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:\text{every }R\text{-module has a projective resolution of length}\le k\}$. By hypothesis $n\in G$, so $G$ is a nonempty set of natural numbers and has a least element $g$ (least number principle, as in Step 2). Every $R$-module has a projective resolution of length $\le g$, and $g\le k$ for every $k\in G$.

source.place: Algebra, Definition Tag 00O4 (definition-finite-proj-dim) and Definition Tag 00O6 (definition-finite-gl-dim); the minima are stated there without proof

proof.text: (3) The equivalence. Let $k\ge0$. If $g\le k$, let $N$ be any $R$-module; by Step 4 it has a projective resolution of length $\le g$, which padded by zeros (Step 1, with $g\le k$) is one of length $\le k$; so every $R$-module has a projective resolution of length $\le k$. Conversely, if every $R$-module has a projective resolution of length $\le k$, then $k\in G$, so $g\le k$ by the minimality of $g$ (Step 4).

split_report.summary: Statement checked against Stacks Definitions 00O4 and 00O6 (algebra.tex, labels definition-finite-proj-dim and definition-finite-gl-dim), which assert the minima without proof; statement kept. Proof written by the agent in five elementary steps: (1) padding by zero modules, checking the complex condition and exactness at the new zeros, at P_n (the incoming map is still zero, so exactness there is the injectivity of d_n from the original sequence) and elsewhere, with the zero module projective as a direct summand of the free module on the empty set [def-weil-pbc-projective-module, def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence]; (2)-(3) the least element d of the nonempty set of lengths by the least number principle of N, and the equivalence via padding and minimality; (4)-(5) the same for the set of global bounds. The well-ordering of N is elementary (lem-weil-pbc-well-ordering-theorem, Zermelo for arbitrary sets, is not needed). No new node. lean.statement: theorem projective_and_global_dimension_well_defined {R : Type u} [CommRing R] (M : ModuleCat.{max u v} R) (m n : ℕ) (hnm : n ≤ m) : (∀ P : ProjectiveResolution M, (∀ i : ℕ, n < i → IsZero (P.complex.X i)) → ∀ i : ℕ, m < i → IsZero (P.complex.X i)) ∧ (HasProjectiveResolutionLE M n → ∃ d : ℕ, HasProjectiveResolutionLE M d ∧ ∀ k : ℕ, HasProjectiveResolutionLE M k ↔ d ≤ k) ∧ ((∃ b : ℕ, Ring.HasGlobalDimensionLE.{u, max u v} R b) → ∃ g : ℕ, Ring.HasGlobalDimensionLE.{u, max u v} R g ∧ ∀ k : ℕ, Ring.HasGlobalDimensionLE.{u, max u v} R k ↔ g ≤ k)
